title: Hugging Face Quiz
description: Revisit the key ideas in Hugging Face. Read each choice carefully. You can try the quiz again after reviewing the lessons.

questions.question: Which library handles the local data tables here?
questions.explanation: Hugging Face includes a Hub for shared resources and libraries used in local programs. These are related tools with different jobs. The list separates the website from the libraries. The examples in this course use only local Datasets and Tokenizers features.

questions.question: What explains the intended use and limits?
questions.explanation: A model card explains a shared model's intended use, training information, checks and limits. Also read its licence and files before deciding to use it. These details help judge whether a model fits a task. A download count is not proof of safety, accuracy or permission for every use.

questions.question: How many rows are created?
questions.explanation: A Dataset holds rows with named columns. from_dict creates a dataset from equally sized lists, one list per column. The result shows three rows and the text and length columns. The first text and first length form one record.

questions.question: Which row appears first in small?
questions.explanation: select makes a dataset containing chosen row positions. Positions begin at zero, and the requested order is preserved. The output is ['stars', 'moon']. Position 2 is selected first and position 0 second. The original dataset is still available.

questions.question: Why is sun not kept?
options: It is always an invalid word
Its length is not greater than 3
questions.explanation: filter keeps rows for which a function returns True. The function receives a row and checks the condition you chose. The output is ['moon', 'stars']. Their lengths are 4 and 5, both greater than 3. sun has length 3 and is removed from this result.

questions.question: What does characters measure here?
questions.explanation: map applies a function to rows and returns an updated dataset. Returning a dictionary can add named fields. The output is [4, 3]. map calculates a character count for each text. The original text column remains in the resulting dataset.

questions.question: How many rows are held out?
questions.explanation: train_test_split divides a dataset into training and test parts. A seed makes this split repeatable for the same data and tool behaviour. The output is 4 2. test_size=2 requests two rows, leaving four for training. This tiny split is only a procedure demonstration.

questions.question: Which ID represents moon?
questions.explanation: A tokenizer turns text into pieces and IDs. WordLevel uses whole pieces from a supplied vocabulary. Whitespace splits this simple sentence into words. The output shows ['moon', 'glows'] and [2, 3]. The vocabulary assigns those IDs, and the pre-tokenizer separates the words before lookup.

questions.question: Why does boat become [UNK]?
options: It has too many letters for every tokenizer
It is absent from the vocabulary
questions.explanation: When a piece is missing from this WordLevel vocabulary, the tokenizer uses its unknown marker. It does not invent a new learned word entry. The output shows ['[UNK]', 'glows'] and [1, 3]. boat is absent, so it becomes the unknown token with ID 1.

questions.question: What does ID 3 decode to?
questions.explanation: Decoding maps known token IDs back to text. Tokenization may not preserve every detail of original spacing, so test exact-text needs carefully. The output is moon glows. IDs 2 and 3 map back to their words. This does not prove the original spaces or formatting can always be recovered.

questions.question: Which mask value marks padding here?
questions.explanation: Padding adds filler tokens to reach a chosen length. An attention mask marks real tokens with 1 and padding with 0 in this encoding. The output is [2, 3, 0, 0] [1, 1, 0, 0]. Two real tokens are followed by two padding tokens. The mask distinguishes them.

questions.question: What is saved by this example?
questions.explanation: A tokenizer can save its settings as a JSON file. Reloading that file restores the local vocabulary and processing rules. The output is [2, 3]. The local file stores the tokenizer setup. No model weights are trained, and nothing is uploaded to the Hub.
